name: Lindquist-Wheeler Lattice Universe
description: A closed universe that holds nothing but $N$ equal masses, one at the centre of each cell of a regular tiling of the three sphere, built by Richard Lindquist and John Wheeler in 1957 from pieces of Schwarzschild's geometry. Fitting the pieces together makes the lattice expand and fall back almost as Friedmann's closed universe of dust does. It is an approximate spacetime, and an early test of whether a universe whose matter comes in lumps expands like a smooth one.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre of each cell. The angle $\psi$ is the angular radius of a cell on the comparison hypersphere, which the number of cells $N$ fixes through $N(2\psi - \sin 2\psi) = 2\pi$.
history: Suppose the universe held no smooth fluid, only a few identical masses, evenly spaced, with vacuum between them. Would it still swell and fall back the way Alexander Friedmann's closed universe of dust does [friedmann1922]? That question came to the Chapel Hill conference of January 1957 with Richard Lindquist, a predoctoral fellow at Princeton [lindquist2011, lindquist1957]. His tool came from the physics of metals: he called it "what is essentially the Wigner-Seitz approximation carried over bodily from solid state physics" [lindquist2011]. He and John Wheeler published the construction in full that July [lindquist1957].¶The approximation cuts a crystal into identical cells, one around each ion, and rounds each cell off to a ball of the same volume [liu2015]. Lindquist and Wheeler did the same to a closed universe [lindquist1957]. A three sphere can be tiled by identical regular cells in six ways, with 5, 8, 16, 24, 120, or 600 of them, so they put a mass at the centre of each cell and filled a ball around it with Karl Schwarzschild's geometry [lindquist1957, clifton2012, schwarzschild1916]. Balls do not tile a sphere, so the lattice is an approximation, and the work lies in fitting them together [clifton2009]. Picture each cell as a funnel pressed against the hypersphere. The lattice holds when, in Lindquist's words, "the Schwarzschild funnels shall be tangent to the hypersphere" [lindquist2011].¶By symmetry a particle midway between two neighbouring masses falls freely, and in Schwarzschild's geometry a shell of such particles climbs, stops, and falls back [clifton2012, clifton2009]. Tangency ties the radius $a$ of the hypersphere to that shell, and $a$ then obeys $\dot{a}^2 = r_s/(a\sin^3\psi) - 1$, Friedmann's equation for dust with its one constant changed [clifton2009]. "One gets from this model an expanding and contracting universe, with a cycloidal behavior," Lindquist reported [lindquist2011]. How far is it from the smooth universe of the same total mass? With five masses the lattice grows to 1.43 times Friedmann's largest radius, and with 600 the two differ by 1.2 percent [clifton2009]. Hermann Bondi asked from the floor how many granules of mass such a universe allows, and answered himself: "Of course it is your number 600" [lindquist2011].¶The lattice came back in 2009 with a question about light [clifton2009]. In a universe of islands a ray spends its whole journey in vacuum, where only tides bend it, so does it report the same distances as a ray through Friedmann's fluid [clifton2009]? Timothy Clifton and Pedro Ferreira sent rays through a flat version of the lattice, cell after cell, and found the redshift $z$ growing more slowly than Friedmann's $z_F$, as $1 + z \simeq (1 + z_F)^{7/10}$ [clifton2009]. They judged the difference a poor candidate to stand in for dark energy [clifton2009].¶One moment of the lattice can be had exactly [clifton2012]. At the instant of greatest expansion nothing moves, Einstein's constraint becomes a linear equation on the three sphere, and its solution for any number of masses is a sum with one term per mass [wheeler1983, clifton2012]. Lindquist told Chapel Hill he had already checked the spacing of his masses against a rigorous solution of that kind, and in 1963 he and Dieter Brill published its flat space counterpart for black holes at rest [lindquist2011, brill1963]. Measured against Friedmann's universe of the same mass, the exact moment with five masses is about a third larger and the one with 600 agrees to better than one percent, in step with the 1957 estimate [clifton2012]. Eloisa Bentivegna and Mikołaj Korzyński then ran the moment with eight masses forward on a computer [bentivegna2012]. For the first third of the collapse, as far as the run could follow, the edge of a cell shrank as a closed Friedmann universe does, one a quarter heavier than its eight black holes together [bentivegna2012].

related.text: Every cell is a piece of Schwarzschild's geometry, cut off at a sphere in radial free fall. The lattice has no other ingredient [lindquist1957].

The smooth universe the lattice is measured against. The comparison hypersphere obeys Friedmann's equation for closed dust, and its largest radius is $3\pi/(2N\sin^3\psi)$ times Friedmann's for the same total mass, which tends to 1 as $N$ grows [clifton2009].

The exact form of one moment. At the instant of greatest expansion the lattice's initial data are Brill and Lindquist's, written on a three sphere in place of flat space, with one term for each mass [brill1963, clifton2012].

The same fit turned inside out. There a ball of Friedmann's dust sits inside Schwarzschild's vacuum, here Schwarzschild's vacuum sits inside a cell of a closed universe, and in both the boundary falls along a radial geodesic whose energy is the cosine of the boundary's angle.
In the exact moment of greatest expansion each mass is the mouth of an Einstein-Rosen bridge, with a sheet of its own on the far side [clifton2012].
Lindquist and Wheeler's comoving coordinates are Tolman and Bondi's with no dust in them: every shell carries the same mass, and the energy function is $E = -r_s/2\rho$.
Many black holes in an expanding universe as an exact solution, which takes a cosmological constant and a charge on every hole equal to its mass [kastor1993].

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild Cell
domains: r = r_b(t) \;\text{(the boundary of the cell)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre of each cell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, a length
Angular radius of a cell on the comparison hypersphere, a pure number with $0 < \psi < \pi/2$, which $N$ cells of equal volume fix through $N(2\psi - \sin 2\psi) = 2\pi$

coordinates.convention: We use Schwarzschild's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ about the mass at the centre of one cell, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. The cell is the ball inside the boundary $r = r_b(t)$, a sphere in radial free fall that turns around at $r_m = r_s/\sin^2\psi$.

coordinates.name: Cosmological Time

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre of each cell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, a length
Square of a comoving shell's energy per unit rest energy, a pure number, $E = \cos^2\psi$ for the lattice of $N$ cells

coordinates.convention: We use Clifton and Ferreira's coordinates $(\tau, r, \theta, \phi)$ inside one cell, where $\tau$ is the proper time of every shell in radial free fall with the boundary's energy, $E = \cos^2\psi$, and $r$ is the areal radius. The signs are those of a cell that expands, and the root changes sign for one that contracts. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{\tau} - \dfrac{r_s\,\sqrt{E\,r - r + r_s}}{2E\,r^{5/2}}\dot{\tau}^2 + \dfrac{r_s}{E\,r^2}\dot{\tau}\dot{r} - \dfrac{r_s}{2E\,r^{3/2}\sqrt{E\,r - r + r_s}}\dot{r}^2 + \sqrt{r}\sqrt{E\,r - r + r_s}\dot{\theta}^2 + \sqrt{r}\sqrt{E\,r - r + r_s}\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Lindquist-Wheeler Comoving

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre of each cell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, a length

Areal radius of the shell labelled $\rho$ at the proper time $\tau$, a length, the cycloid $r = \tfrac{\rho}{2}(1 + \cos\eta)$, $c\tau = \tfrac{\rho}{2}\sqrt{\rho/r_s}\,(\eta + \sin\eta)$ in a parameter $\eta \in (-\pi, \pi)$; no component assumes it

coordinates.convention: We use Lindquist and Wheeler's comoving coordinates $(\tau, \rho, \theta, \phi)$ inside one cell, where $\rho$ labels a shell in radial free fall by the largest radius it reaches, $\tau$ is its proper time counted from that moment, and $r(\tau, \rho)$ is its areal radius. Each shell obeys $(\partial_\tau r)^2 = r_s/r - r_s/\rho$ with $\partial_\tau = c^{-1}\partial/\partial\tau$, and the boundary of the cell is the shell $\rho = r_m = r_s/\sin^2\psi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, so $\dot{\tau}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Comparison Hypersphere

parameters.description: Radius of the comparison hypersphere, a length, the cycloid $a = \tfrac{a_m}{2}(1 + \cos\eta)$, $c\tau = \tfrac{a_m}{2}(\eta + \sin\eta)$ in a parameter $\eta \in (-\pi, \pi)$, with the largest radius $a_m = r_s/\sin^3\psi$; no component assumes it
Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre of each cell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, a length
Angular radius of a cell on the comparison hypersphere, a pure number with $0 < \psi < \pi/2$, which $N$ cells of equal volume fix through $N(2\psi - \sin 2\psi) = 2\pi$

coordinates.convention: We use hyperspherical coordinates $(\tau, \chi, \theta, \phi)$ on the comparison hypersphere of radius $a(\tau)$, where $\tau$ is the proper time of the cell boundaries and $\chi$ is the angle from the centre of one cell, whose boundary $\chi = \psi$ has the areal radius $a\sin\psi$. A dot on the radius is $\dot{a} = \dfrac{1}{c}\dfrac{da}{d\tau}$, and the lattice obeys $\dot{a}^2 = \dfrac{r_s}{a\sin^3\psi} - 1$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, so $\dot{\tau}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
